**Vignette: Priya**

Priya is a 43-year-old South Asian woman who has worked as a licensed plumber for nearly fifteen years. She built her reputation quietly but steadily — reliable, technically precise, the kind of tradesperson other contractors call when a job is complicated. She takes pride in her work and, until two years ago, she loved it.

Two years ago, Priya was contracted to repair a corroded drainage system in the basement of an older commercial building. No one told her the property had previously housed a dry-cleaning operation. No one mentioned the residual solvent contamination still pooling in the subfloor. She was working alone in an enclosed space when the smell hit her — sharp, chemical, almost sweet — and within minutes she was dizzy, her eyes burning, her throat tightening. She tried to move toward the stairs and found she couldn't coordinate her legs properly. She collapsed before she reached them. A delivery worker found her forty minutes later, unresponsive. She was hospitalized for six days with chemical toxicity affecting her respiratory system and liver function. Doctors were cautious with their language, but Priya understood enough to know that those forty minutes alone on that floor could have killed her.

Physically, she recovered — or at least her bloodwork eventually said she did. But something shifted in the weeks after discharge that has never shifted back. The first time she tried to return to work, she arrived at a job site, opened the door to a utility room, and smelled something she couldn't even name — perhaps just old pipe, perhaps cleaning solution left by a janitor — and her body responded as though she were back on that basement floor. Her heart slammed against her chest, her vision narrowed, and she was out on the sidewalk before she consciously decided to leave. She sat in her van for two hours, shaking, unable to explain to her client why she had gone.

That pattern has become her life. She still works — she forces herself, because the business is hers and her family depends on it — but every enclosed space is now a negotiation between what she knows intellectually and what her body insists is true. Crawl spaces are nearly impossible. Basements require her to stand at the threshold for several minutes, running through a mental checklist that never fully quiets the alarm rising in her chest. She has started leaving jobs early, rescheduling clients, turning down work she would once have taken without hesitation. Her apprentice has noticed, though he hasn't said anything directly.

At home, Priya is present in body but often somewhere else entirely. Her husband, Rajan, describes her as "gone behind the eyes" some evenings. She startles when he comes up behind her, then feels ashamed of the look on his face — concern edging toward helplessness. She doesn't sleep through the night. She wakes between two and four in the morning with her heart already racing, sometimes mid-dream, sometimes from nothing she can identify. The dreams are not always literal replays; sometimes she is simply trapped somewhere dark, unable to move, knowing something is wrong with the air.

She has not told her parents or her in-laws what happened. In her family, illness is managed quietly, and psychological struggle even more so. She describes feeling like she is "performing being fine" at family gatherings, which leaves her exhausted in a way that is different from physical fatigue. She has begun avoiding social obligations, finding reasons not to attend events that once grounded her.

What troubles Priya most, she says, is the sense that she no longer trusts herself. She used to read a space — its pressures, its risks — and feel confident in her own judgment. Now she doesn't know whether what she's sensing is real danger or her own mind misfiring. That uncertainty, more than the nightmares or the sleeplessness, is what she finds hardest to carry.
